about: AMPLE mix starting points (MT01): per instrument kind and genre, the first levels, pan, filter, EQ, compression and sends to try before listening and adjusting. They are starting points, not rules: set them, run ample_listen, then change by ear. Original numbers for AMPLE; no preset of another product.
units: level = gain of a volume block in dB (0 is unchanged); pan = the pan block, -32 (left) to 32 (right); highpass = a filter block type highpass with cutoff in Hz; eq = the eq block (low, mid, high in dB around low_hz and high_hz); comp = compressor threshold dB and ratio; reverb and delay = the mix percent of a send or effect.

master.note: Keep the sum of the blocks peaking around -6 dBFS before the master limiter (ceiling -1 dB); a quiet mix plus a limiter sounds better than a loud mix squashed by it.

order: 1. Set the kick and the bass first (they carry the low end), then the snare or clap, then the rest of the drums.
2. Bring in the main melodic instrument and set it against the drums.
3. Add pads, strings and textures well below the main instrument; they fill, they do not lead.
4. Last the vocal or the lead: it sits on top, everything else steps back under it.
5. Pan the supporting parts, leave kick, bass and lead vocal in the middle.
6. Check the whole: the master peak, ample_listen, then turn everything down together if it is too hot.

instruments.notes: Centre. Loudest of the drums. A little reverb only on a snare or clap, never on the kick.
Centre; a short plate-like reverb gives it size.
Often layered with the snare; slightly wider reverb.
Quiet and a little off-centre; if it hisses, lower the high EQ.
Pan opposite the closed hat.
Spread low to high from the left to the right for fills.
Pan off-centre; keep it low so it adds motion, not weight.
Centre. No reverb. Make the kick and bass share the low end: duck the bass under the kick.
Mono and clean. Use it with a regular bass above it, not on top of the kick.
Slightly off-centre; cut the low end under 80 Hz so the bass has room.
Pan opposite a guitar. A little chorus or tremolo adds width.
Keep it behind the main instrument.
A single guitar can sit left; two guitars go left and right.
Double-track and pan hard left and right for width; keep the vocal clear in the mids.
Well below the lead; cut the mids so it does not mask the voice or the piano.
A swell works best for build-ups and the last chorus.
On top of the mix; a dotted-eighth delay gives it movement without clutter.
Quieter than the lead; pan to one side.
Short stabs on the off-beat; keep them out of the vocal's way.
Centre, loudest melodic element; make room for it by cutting 2 to 4 kHz from the instruments around it.
Wider and softer than the lead, with more reverb.
A rhythmic delay turns a short chop into a groove; keep it out of the vocal's range.
Match its tempo and key to the song first; then set its level against the kick.
Quiet bed under a change of section; automate its level if you can.

notes: The kick leads; duck the bass and the pad from it (a duck block fed by the kick).
Keep the percussion bright and quiet; build by adding one layer at a time.
Kick and sub bass are the weight; keep the vocal dry and loud.
Short, tight reverbs: a long tail muddies the beat.
Everything soft and a little dull: lower the high EQ on all parts by 2 to 3 dB.
A quiet vinyl-like noise bed and gentle compression give the feel.
Snare and vocal are the centre; pan two guitars hard left and right.
Tight and dry: bass and kick lock together; the guitar is short and percussive.
The bass is the lead; the off-beat guitar skank is short and quiet.
A tape-like delay on the snare and organ is part of the sound.
Sub bass and snare dominate; keep the sub mono and clean.
The voice and the main instrument are everything; the drums stay far below.
More reverb on voice and strings, none on the kick and bass.
Acoustic guitar and voice lead; a pedal steel or fiddle sits to one side.
Natural dynamics: little compression; the ride and the bass carry the time.
Long reverbs and slow movement; leave silence and dynamics alone.
